findings.evidence: "Riders may request a fare adjustment through the mobile app. Station staff can also help with the same request in person."
findings.fix: Replace this paragraph with actual accessibility-related content (e.g., elevator status, ramp availability) or move it to a relevant section like fares.
findings.violation: The content has nothing to do with accessibility; it describes a fare-adjustment process under a heading promising accessibility information.

findings.evidence: "Passengers can check real time arrivals by calling rider services. Updates post to the schedule page within one business day."
findings.fix: Move this content to a "Real-time arrivals" or "Schedule" section, and add genuine accessibility content here.
findings.violation: Again, this is about real-time arrival info, not accessibility, so the section heading is not supported by its content.

findings.evidence: "Passengers may request a fare adjustment through the mobile app. Station staff can also help with the same request in person."
findings.fix: Remove the duplicated fare-adjustment text and replace it with actual weekend service details (hours, frequency changes, etc.).
findings.violation: This is a near-verbatim duplicate of s1-p1 and is unrelated to "Weekend service," indicating boilerplate copy-paste rather than section-specific content.

findings.fix: Add `<caption>Weekend service status by zone</caption>` as the first child of the table.
findings.violation: The table has no `<caption>` or accessible name, so screen reader users encounter it without knowing what it represents.

findings.evidence: "Local residents should review the updated schedule through the mobile app. Station staff can also help with the same request in person."
findings.fix: Rewrite the sentence to match the actual action, e.g., "Station staff can also provide the updated schedule in person."
findings.violation: The second sentence ("help with the same request") was copy-pasted from the fare-adjustment boilerplate and doesn't logically follow "review the updated schedule" - reviewing a schedule isn't a "request" staff can help fulfill in the same sense.

findings.evidence: "Passengers should review the updated schedule through the mobile app. The change takes effect on the following service day."
findings.fix: Merge s3-p1 and s3-p2 into one non-repetitive paragraph, or differentiate their content clearly.
findings.violation: The first sentence duplicates s3-p1's opening sentence almost verbatim, producing redundant content within the same section.

findings.evidence: "Route adjustments take effect on the posted effective date."
findings.fix: State the concrete effective date or link to where riders can find it, e.g., "Route adjustments take effect on November 3."
findings.violation: This statement is circular/tautological (an "effective date" is by definition when something takes effect) and conveys no actual information to the rider.

findings.evidence: "Local residents can check real time arrivals by calling rider services. Updates post to the schedule page within one business day."
findings.fix: Remove the duplicate and keep real-time arrival info consolidated in one place.
findings.violation: This duplicates s1-p2 almost word-for-word, appearing in an unrelated section ("Schedule changes") a second time.

findings.fix: Either remove this control if unused, or implement it as a `<button>` with a descriptive accessible name (e.g., `aria-label="Delete"`), and confirm it belongs on this page.
findings.violation: This is an interactive-looking "delete" control implemented as a non-interactive `<div>` with an image that has empty alt text, making it unreachable by keyboard and unlabeled for screen readers; it's also thematically unrelated to a transit schedule page (looks like leftover e-commerce UI).

findings.fix: Reorder the DOM elements to match the intended logical sequence instead of relying on CSS `order` to fix visual order.
findings.violation: The visual order (via CSS `order`) reads "Choose a plan → Enter payment details → Confirm your order," but the underlying DOM/reading order is reversed, so screen reader and keyboard-navigation users encounter the steps out of sequence (WCAG 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence violation).

findings.evidence: "Confirm your order", "Enter payment details", "Choose a plan"
findings.fix: Remove this wizard block or replace it with content relevant to transit schedule changes.
findings.violation: This checkout/payment-flow content ("order," "payment details," "plan") is thematically unrelated to a transit route-update page and appears to be leftover template content from an e-commerce checkout flow.

findings.evidence: `For the full list of upcoming adjustments, read the accessibility improvements list.`
findings.fix: Rewrite the link text to accurately describe the destination, e.g., "view fare history," or correct the href to match the described content.
findings.violation: The link text ("accessibility improvements list") contradicts both the surrounding sentence ("full list of upcoming adjustments") and the destination URL (`/fares/history`), making the link's purpose unclear and misleading.

findings.fix: Add explicit text (e.g., "Phone number (required)") or an `aria-required="true"` attribute alongside the visual styling.
findings.violation: Red coloring is used as the sole indicator that this field is required (or otherwise significant), which fails WCAG 1.4.1 (use of color) since the meaning isn't conveyed to users who can't perceive color or color alone.

findings.fix: Add `aria-describedby="s3-form-promo-error"` to the input, write a descriptive message (e.g., "Promo code is invalid or expired"), and only set `aria-invalid="true"` after validation fails.
findings.violation: The error message "Error." is not descriptive (fails WCAG 3.3.1) and is not programmatically associated with the input via `aria-describedby`, so screen reader users won't know what's wrong or that the message relates to this field; additionally the field is marked invalid by default before any user interaction.

findings.evidence: "Riders may request..." (s1-p1) vs. "Passengers may request..." (s2-p1) vs. "Local residents should review..." (s3-p1)
findings.fix: Standardize on one term (e.g., "riders") throughout the document.
findings.violation: The document inconsistently refers to its audience as "riders," "passengers," and "local residents," which reads as unedited boilerplate rather than a coherent voice.
